rules.quote: Don’t add full stops to the ends of headings, page headers, footers or captions.
rules.violation_condition: A heading, page header, footer or caption ends with a full stop.
when: Applies to headings, page headers, footers and captions.
rules.why: G-1: the specific punctuation checks are rules; their introductory heading is a section. G-2: the listed locations are cases of the same check.

rules.quote: Don’t use a semicolon at the end of each item in a bullet list.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list item has a semicolon as its terminal punctuation.
when: Applies to bullet-list items, not semicolons within an item's text.
rules.why: G-1: this is a specific check under the minimal-punctuation introduction.

rules.quote: Unless each item is a full sentence or the last item in a list, don’t use a full stop for items in bullet lists.
rules.violation_condition: A non-final bullet-list item ends with a full stop when the list does not consist of full sentences.
when: Applies to bullet lists.
Except where each item is a full sentence.
Except for the last item in a list.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: full-sentence lists and final items are exceptions to one terminal-full-stop check.

rules.quote: Don’t use full stops between letters in an acronym or initialism.
rules.violation_condition: An acronym or initialism contains full stops between its letters.
when: The letters form an acronym or initialism.
rules.why: G-1: internal punctuation in shortened forms is a distinct check, not another formulation of list or heading punctuation.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop at the end of most abbreviations.
rules.specification: The page does not identify the abbreviations covered by ‘most’ or list the exceptions. An exception inventory is needed before reliable findings can be issued.
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviation has a terminal full stop despite not belonging to the permitted exceptional forms.
when: Applies to a full stop belonging to the abbreviation, not a full stop independently required to end a sentence.
Exceptional abbreviations are excluded, but this page does not identify them.
rules.why: G-2: the unspecified exceptional abbreviations belong within one terminal-punctuation rule.

rules.quote: Include a single space after a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence.
rules.specification: Interpret this as a separating space between sentences in running text, not trailing whitespace at a paragraph boundary or a space inside closing quotation marks. Multiple spaces are checked by the separate prohibition on double spaces.
rules.violation_condition: Consecutive sentences in running text have no separating space after the first sentence's closing punctuation.
when: Another sentence follows in the same paragraph.
Closing quotation marks or brackets remain attached to the preceding sentence.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: the body supplies the actionable spacing requirement. Missing spacing is separated from the following prohibition on multiple spaces so the checks do not overlap.

covers.quote: Check each document for double and multiple spaces and delete them.

rules.violation_condition: The text contains two or more consecutive spaces.

rules.quote: Capitalise the first word in a sentence. Use lower case for all other words, unless those words include proper nouns.
rules.specification: Treat sentence case as one check across the listed contexts, including the prohibition on unnecessary capitals in common-noun expansions and role names. Specific rules govern proper-name expansions, official titles before names, measurement symbols and legislatively defined forms; do not issue duplicate general-case findings for those forms. The page leaves some exceptions to other guidance, and the all-capital-heading exception needs evidence about visual design.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence, opening quoted-speech passage, heading or referenced work title has a lower-case first word, or contains capitals on words that should be lower case, outside the stated exceptions and specific capitalisation conventions.
when: Applies to sentences, the opening of quoted speech within a sentence, headings and titles of works mentioned in content.
The title-of-work requirement also applies when the title appears in a heading.
Proper nouns are exempt from the general lower-case requirement.
Adjectives referring to national, religious or linguistic groups can have capitals.
An acronym or initialism's capitals do not by themselves justify capitals in a common-noun full form.
Organisational positions and roles in body text use lower case unless this manual advises otherwise.
Deferential capitals permitted by an organisation's house style are limited to that organisational context.
All-capital headings are excepted only when the visual design meets WCAG in all respects.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: sentence case, unnecessary capitals on common words, common-noun expansions and organisational roles share the same case check. G-3: the stated capitalisation exceptions limit that check.

rules.quote: Use sentence case with italics for titles of works mentioned in the content.
rules.specification: This item checks italics only. The sentence-case requirement in the same sentence is consolidated into the general sentence-case rule.
rules.violation_condition: A referenced title of a work is not italicised.
when: A title of a work is mentioned in the content.
Applies even when the reference appears within a heading.
rules.why: The grain test separates missing italics from incorrect capitalisation: either can be wrong independently. G-2: titles within headings are a condition of the same italics check.

when: The text uses a shortened form.

tags.violation_condition: An official title preceding its office holder's name lacks the capitals required for that title.

when: An official title precedes the office holder's name.
Includes titles for executives specified in legislation.
Capitalisation is not required merely because a title is an organisational name given to an office holder.
rules.why: G-2: executive titles specified in legislation are included in the same positional check. G-3: organisational titles are not automatically subject to the requirement.

anchor.quote: In these cases, use the form of the name as it is written in the legislation.

covers.quote: Legal documents often use initial capitals to show terms with a defined meaning (such as ‘Department’, ‘Schedule’, ‘Vendor’ and ‘Recipient’).

tags.violation_condition: A legislatively defined name or term is written in a form that differs from its form in the legislation.

when: Legal content uses a legislatively defined name or term whose initial capitals signal its defined meaning.
